My hon. friend from St. John has known Sir Ezekiel McLeod for years. I have known him since I was old enough to know public men. Will my hon. friend from 6t. John admit that Sir Ezekiel McLeod is a dishonest man?
Would the hon. member like to lead us in prayer?

That would be
something so entirely foreign to anything the hon. gentleman from Carleton knows anything about, that it would be useless to do it; however, I should say the words of the prayer he would use are so well known that it is unnecessary to repeat them. They would be those of the Pharisee: "I thank thee, Lord, that I am not as other men." I cannot possibly understand the hon. gentle-, man making the statement he has made with reference to the honesty of these gentlemen, One would think that he was counsel against Mr. Rogers and for the Hon. Mr. Justice Galt and in that capacity was saying " The conclusion the appeal court arrived at is Totten." When I was a young man and used to learn much from the hon. member from St. John (Mr. Pugsley)
I am afraid you have gone astray.

No. I have never forgotten many of the lessons that I learned, but the lesson of urbanity I have never yet been able to learn. I have never been able to say "Thank you" with that eame kind consideration that he does. I should like to, but I fear I never shall.
You have not practised enough. .

I have not, to the same extent. But this was a fundamental lesson, that courts of appeal sometimes decide against us. I can remember cases in which, as counsel, the hon. member for St. John sometimes buoyed me up with

high hope that possibly we might succeed. I have known cases in which the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) was interested in which we were buoyed up with high hope. When we succeeded before the trial judge, we went on, with hope still springing eternal in the human breast, to the court of appeal, and that court decided against us-and we were wrong, the trial judge was wrong. But it is not usual for counsel, in cases like that, to stand up and charge the tribunal with arriving at a conclusion which no honest man would arrive at.
Has the hon. gentleman not had experience that would induce him to believe that sometimes, after all, the judgment of the lowest court was the best judgment?
There have been cases in which we still thought so.
Yes.
But we were bound by the decision of the Appellate Court.
This is not a court of appeal.

And has not the hon. gentleman known of cases where a third or final Appellate Court has reversed the findings of the first Appellate Court? Therefore, would it not be well to appoint another tribunal to try the findings of the first appeal court?
Unfortunately, as the law stands, there is no provision for a higher tribunal.
Nor was there for this.
Does the hon. member agree with the Secretary of State that this Government had power, without a reference to Parliament, to appoint a second tribunal under the Inquiries Act?

I tried to make clear in my few remarks a moment ago why any tribunal was appointed. The Inquiries Act enables us to create machinery and, to issue, under the Great Seal, a commission to inquire into a question. The Inquiries Act is a part of the statute law of this country. It- is there for that very purpose. Being there, we took advantage of the machinery of that statute for the purpose indicated by the Secretary of State (Mr. Meighen) and by myself, namely to determine whether or not the honour of this Parliament would in any sense be offended

through, these charges against one of its members being supported by any evidence. That is all.
Does the hon. member not think that the Inquiries Act makes provision for the initiation of investigations of this kind, and not for courts of review?

What my hon. friend has said would certainly be entirely in order were it not for one fact, and that is that this, was a provincial matter and the inquiry was with respect to wrong-doing alleged during the term of office of a provincial minister.
It is the same King in Manitoba that we have here.
The only King my friend knows sits directly to his right, and I do not think he sits for Manitoba.
There are greater things than these.

But the same King unquestionably, as my friend the judge (Mr. McKenzie) has said, but there is no appeal from the findings with respect to a provincial matter to another tribunal in that sense, so we had to create some tribunal to make the inquiry for this Parliament, and the inquiry it made was an inquiry de novo as to the extent to which, if any, there was any evidence upon which to predicate those findings.

Would it not have been better for the Government to have instituted an inquiry de novo to take the evidence either in Manitoba or here, probably by sending the judges to Manitoba, and then have counsel on both sides, and have the judges see the witnesses? Would'that not have been the better course to pursue?

I am sorry to say that that course would have been entirely unconstitutional. It would not have been within the ambit of our powers to intrude ourselves upon matters which were purely provincial in their character. We have no right to make that inquiry.
Hear, hear.

That is exactly what I was desirous my hon. friends would say. They are angry and balked because a public man has not been permitted to lie under an unfounded and unwarranted aspersion upon his character.

That is what is the
matter with them.

That is the whole story, and I feel quite sure that, with the great wealth of experience that their right hon. leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) enjoys, he will be the first man to say that if any machinery can be created and put in motion that will make it clear, not to some other tribunal but to this Parliament, whether or not there is any foundation for the conclusion arrived at with respect to one of its members, that machinery should be used, and used promptly. To that extent it seems to me we are on common ground. Now they complain because the tribunal has found in favour of the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works. That is the whole complaint.
There is no complaint of that.
I quite understand that the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has no complaint as to that, but I am talking now about the hon. member for Carleton and those who take that view.

I made no complaint
whatever. I care nothing whatever. I complain because we are called upon to pay 85,500 for something that was none of our business, but a purely personal matter between Mr. Rogers and his friends in Manitoba.

Let me give an
analogy. I am a member of a club. The question of the expulsion of members of clubs engages the attention of the courts in England more than it does here, but it occasionally does so here, as for instance in connection with the Garrison Club of Quebec. This House of Commons is a club. The people have elected us here. The analogy is complete, and this club of members has the right to expel from its membership any member against whom charges are preferred or findings made that would indicate that he was unfit to be a member of this Parliament, or this club.
In dealing with members of clubs, is it not a judgment of the members of the club itself that is passed upon the erring member, if he does err?
Precisely, except that the committee of the club is usually charged with the duty of making investigation.
Messrs Justice McLeod and Justice Tellier are not members of this club.

But Parliament
constituted them a committee to act and to determine that matter because they aTe judicial in their character, and this club, unlike the ordinary social club, is torn into two or more factions by political differences.

But from that you
must not presume that this Parliament would not fairly try one of its members. That is a wild presumption.

I am not making presumptions of that character, but I am sure any judicial inquiry is 'to be preferred to one by members torn by distracting questions and partisans in their character admittedly, as we are-and no man has made a stronger statement in respect to that than the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie).
This House, under the authority of the Inquiries Act, has seen fit to create a small committee, consisting of two eminent judges, and charged them with the responsibility-not as my hon. friend suggests, of going down to Manitoba and inquiring into a provincial matter-but of determining whether or not, on the evidence given before that tribunal, there was any evidence to go to the jury of the guilt of the person charged.

If there is any objection to the commission composed of Chief Justice McLeod and Mr. Justice Tellier going into the province of Manitoba, there is ample provision, under the Inquiries Act, to bring the evidence here. Let them sit here.

My dear, learned and honourable friend, the ex-judge, is too astute a man, too subtle-minded for a single moment to think it was a question of geography I was dealing with. I was dealing with jurisdiction, and he knew it as well as I knew it. He knew that this Parliament should not be intruding itself into provincial matters that affected provincial administration only.
My hon. friend, who is a big lawyer-
No,-not now.
-says they would have no jurisdiction if they heard the evidence de novo, but they have jurisdiction if they read the evidence and report. Is that the logic of my hon. friend?

No, no. My hon. friend knows what I mean. I can see by

the colour of his face that he appreciates the position.
It is past me, I cannot understand it.

The hon. gentleman knows it is purely a question of jurisdiction. The Legislature of Manitoba has plenary powers, and this Parliament, under its constitution, also has plenary powers. The Legislature of Manitoba create a commission to inquire into the administration of its own affairs.
This Parliament has nothing to do with the administration of the Public Works Department of Manitoba, but has to do with the honour of one of its members, and, based upon the assumption that a member of this House had been found guilty of malfeasance in his administration in the provincial government-that having been certified to as a fact-this Parliament created the tribunal to consider whether or not any evidence had been adduced which would justify such finding, the accused having said that there was no evidence to justify if. This Parliament has no right to go down to the province of New Brunswick, and to inquire into the Public Works Department there. If it did, it would have a lively time, but it would have no power to do so.
During the last five years there would be considerable to investigate.
The administration of the last five years would not compare with the administration of the days long past.
They are not doing badly as it is.

And as long as it continues my hon. friend from Carleton will find some scope for his activities, and will be able to earn a good fee. But I want to emphasize the fact that we, as a Parliament, could not inquire into the Public Works Department of Manitoba, and that one of our members having been assailed, and found guilty of an offence in Manitoba, it became our duty to determine whether we should let it go, or have a decent and proper tribunal review the finding and determine whether there was any evidence to sustain it. That tribunal has declared there was no evidence, and now against that finding, the hon, gentleman from Carleton says no honest man should have so found it. Is that a proper way in which to approach this matter? I am sure the hon. member for St.

John would have been better pleased, his reputation as a public man would have stood much higher in years to come, and the perspective would have been better when the history of our country is written, when we are long gone, if a proper tribunal had reviewed the Landry report, rather than that a partisan majority should vote that these charges against him were wholly unwarranted. The Landry report found the member for St. John guilty-he says falsely. The report to-day stands uncontroverted.

And the Government
counsel said it was false.

But it stands
to-day. The hon. gentleman sits in this House with that finding against him. Whenever he rises im his place to speak in this House, he speaks ias one against whom a finding has been made, and why? Because the Government of the day never appointed a tribunal to inquire whether or not there was any evidence to warrant that finding, and the reason is because they dare not do so. That is the whole story. Everybody knows that. The partisan majority stood up, 'and said: "We shall have no investigation, let the false charge stand against him forever," and he stands in the eyes of public men of this country for all time, in successive generations, as one who is guilty.
And never whitewashed.

Never whitewashed, because whitewashing would be absolutely useless. No process of whitewashing would accomplish any result. There it istands forever. That is not the course that was pursued by the ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers), a member of this House. He wrote a letter to the country and said "I abandon my portfolio, I resign my position and I want to go out."
He just stood aside for the time being, and was still minister. He kept his portfolio?
My hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) did not do that. Mr. Rogers stood aside and said: I am not guilty of the charges Judge Galt made against me, I demand an inquiry by some tribunal.
It was not an inquiry.
It was an inquiry, because it had to determine whether or not there was any evidence upon which the Galt findings might be predicated, and anything that determines that is :an inquiry.
Not under the Act.

The question was, was there any evidence on which the Galt findings could be predicated so far as Mr. Rogers was concerned. The hon. member from Carleton said I had not read the evidence. I read the evidence as it came out from day to day, and followed that evidence. I may not be as well able to arrive at conclusions as the hon. gentleman from Carleton, but when the conclusions of Mr. Justice Galt were arrived at I failed-and I have failed ever since-to put my finger on the evidence upon which those conclusions could have been predicated. That illustrates the difference in view between my hon. friend and myself, and shows the soundness of appointing men absolutely removed from the scene and away from political influence. That is the reason Chief Justice McLeod and Mr. Justice Tellier were appointed. What a lovely mess it would have been if we had appointed members of this House to investigate.
You had a majority in this House and could put good men upon that committee.

We do not find
our ministers innocent by majority.
Perhaps you could not get a majority.

There was no
trouble when my hon. friend was in power in getting a majority. The dark lantern was in evidence in season and out of season. If it were a sawdust wharf, there was no trouble
There was no charge about the sawdust wharf.

Or if it were a
question of the ballot papers of that gentleman named Lott-not the Lot my hon. friend knows so well in Scriptures, whose wife was turned to salt, hut the Lott .who was connected with the ballot boxes, and the ballot papers. On that side of the House you always acquit by majority. We find our men innocent by judges. That is the difference.
You choose your own magistrate.

And we chose a chief magistrate, and one who knows the Scriptures as well as my hon. friend from Cape Breton. My hon. friend speaks of the prophet Ezekiel. (My hon. friend from Carleton refers to prophets, but he spells it with an " f ".) I submit that on the state-

merit made by my hon. friend from Cape Breton the case is complete.
Which case is that?

The case I am making for Mr. Rogers, and this Government. I will admit there was completeness also in the case established against the hon. gentlemen from St. John. I have no doubt that is what he refers to. Here we have my hon. friend standing in his place, and saying " What we want is an acquittal by a partisan majority."
What we say is that we want the reverse, a judicial tribunal, to determine whether our ministers are falsely or properly charged with these offences. The judicial tribunal has made its report, and it ill becomes any gentleman practising his profession as a lawyer" to charge men with whitewashing who have had the administrative and judicial experience of Sir Ezekiel McLeod and Mr. Justice Tellder. I do think this Parliament should rise beyond that. To-morrow some hon. gentleman opposite, 'having become a minister of the Crown may find himself in a similar position. If the leader of the Opposition were called upon to form a government. I have no doubt that he would exercise the same discretion that he did in years gone by. Knowing how unfit was the material he had behind him, he would go to the provinces and get men to form hie government; he could not form a government with men of the type of the Carvells, the McKenzies, the Oopps, the Carrolls and the Pugsleys.

But I had
heard that the Prime Minister wanted to rule with Carvell.
Hear, hear.
Judging from the applause with which that remark was greeted what my right hon. friend says may be so.	[DOT]

I would not
have to go so far, then, as my hon. friend says.

My right hon.
friend has that great quality, that commanding quality, which has always characterized him-it is almost genius-of inducing those with whom he has been associated to believe that in the event of his coming into power every one of them would be fit to hold a position in the Government. But alas, when the moment comes, the fruit is found to be the apple of Sodom; and when his eager followers come to taste

it, they find that it turns to ashes on their lips. My Tight hon. friend under these circumstances would do what he did of old- go outside for his Blairs, his Mowats and his Fieldings.
They filled the positions well.

Yes, they filled
the positions with great distinction and with high honour to themselves and to the country which they served. I have no doubt that those who sit behind my right hon. friend now are anxiously waiting for the day when, they think an ill-guided people may put them into power, and when each of them will become ministers. I can tell by the look of profound wisdom on the face of the member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) that he would fill the office of Marine and Fisheries with distinction. I can imagine the member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) wondering whether he will again adorn the Bench, fill some portfolio or, peradventure, serve the State in a lesser capacity. I can see the member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) vieing with the member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) as to which shall be which; as to who shall be the greater in Israel. I can see the member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) vieing with the member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) and endeavouring to determine which shall represent the great province of Nova Scotia if, peradventure, the member for Guysborough is overlooked. But when the great day comes, they will all find themselves beyond the pale.
I hope that the Chairman is making a note of this discussion. The hon. gentleman is going rather far afield.
I suppose it is all in order.
Entirely in order.
Admitting all that the hon. gentleman has said, I would ask him to justify the proposal to ask the people of Canada to pay for the vindicating of the character of Mr. Rogers.

I was just illustrating my argument. I was pointing out that some hon. gentlemen opposite were hoping to fill positions of responsibility in the State. I hope that some day they may. It is in the interest of the State that they should, so that they may once more illustrate by their performances in office their unfitness for the positions. I was pointing out that if a minister of the Crown

from Nova Scotia should by a commission of inquiry be found guilty of malfeasance, the Government of the day should have the strength, the power and the courage to say: We will appoint a commission to determine whether or not the findings made were justified by the evidence, in order that the public life of our public men may not become the subject of attack 'by every man who wishes to throw mud from any quarter. The hon. Mr. Rogers, despite what may be said, had the courage to ask this Parliament to determine, by tribunal, whether-
Oh, oh.
-this Parliament, and this Government, ig whose hands the honour of Parliament rests for the time being-
Heaven help this Parliament, then.

Well, I would
rather trust a matter of this kind to a competent tribunal than leave it to the judgment of a partisan majority, as was the case with the hon. member for St. John.
The hon. gentleman is prejudiced.

No, not prejudiced,
merely biased. After all, those who occupy high office and discharge public trust must have an opportunity to have themselves vindicated if charges made against them are deemed to be unfounded. I believe that if the member for St. John had his way, he would rather that the charge preferred against him and the finding made should have been reviewed by a competent tribunal under the Inquiries Act than that his name and fame should rest entirely upon a partisan majority's view. Of course, in his case the evidence was so conclusive that no tribunal would ever change the original finding; but he would have liked to have the finding reviewed for the sake of history and his place in it. It is too bad that that matter must rest upon the judgment of a partisan majority rather than upon the judgment of justices who are sworn fairly to administer justice and law. Mr. Roger's case is safe in the finding of Sir Ezekiel McLeod and Mr. Justice Tellier, despite the fact that the member for Carleton says that the conclusions which the Commissioners reached are not such as any honest man could accept.

What has the hon. gentleman to say about the fact that hon.
Mr. Rogers refused to submit any evidence before Mr. Justice Galt, after he was asked to do so?
That is hardly the fact.
That is on record.
No.
Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: He was asked to appear in argument only after the evidence was in.

I desire to express my sympathy with the Solicitor General in the fact that lias estimates are being obstructed by the member for Calgary. He has spoken about almost everything under the sun except the matter which is immediately before the committee. The member for Calgary says that he has learned many things from me; there is one thing that he did not learn: to curtail his speeches in the House. Another thing he did not learn was to say the right thing in the Tight place. If my hon. friend ever did an injustice in his life to any friend he did it today to the ex-Minister of Public Works. He has brought into the consideration of this item the question whether the report of Mr. Justice Galt is sustained hy the evidence. That was not an issue until the hon. gentleman rose in his place and made the very extraordinary speech which he delivered to the committee. He has put squarely before the committee the question whether the finding of Mr. Justice Galt was or was not justified by the evidence. My hon. friend, a prominent member of the House, a warm supporter of the Government, a gentleman occupying a position which many people thought would be second in importance only to that of the Prime Minister-Chairman of the National Service Board-eulogizes the finding of the IMcLeod-Tellier Commission and discredits the finding of Commissioner Galt. The member for Carleton, therefore, takes the right course in claiming the right to have a full discussion of the matter dealt with in this item.
Is my hon. friend aware of the fact that the hon. member for Carleton (M. Carvell) raised the issue before I came into the Chamber?

Not at all.
Mr. R. B. BENNETT [DOT] Well, I heard a part of it.

All that the hon. member for Carleton pointed out was, as I understand his argument, that there wras no authority,

under the Inquiries Act, for the issue of this commission, and he did not see why the country should be called upon to pay the expenses of it and particularly the fee of the counsel employed to assist the commissioners in arriving at a conclusion. The view I take of this matter is that we have no judgment of a court. The expression of opinion by Mr. Justice Galt is not a judgment of the court; neither is the expression of opinion by Chief Justice McLeod or exjudge Tellier a judgment of a court. They are simply expressions of opinion by those gentlemen which will have no weight and which ought to have no weight either with the people of this country or with the members of this Parliament unless the evidence justifies either the one or the other. That is all. The one is the expression of opinion of two very worthy gentlemen, and the other is the expression of opinion of a gentleman who was appointed, on the recommendation of the ex-Minister of Public Works, to the very high office of judge because of his great ability and integrity, and presumably also because of his impartiality. We have one opinion one way and another opinion the other way. The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. E. B. Bennett) appealed to me as to whether or not Chief Justice McLeod could be suspected for a moment of coming to a wrong or improper conclusion or of dishonesty. I would be the last man in the world to suggest such a thing with regard to -Chief Justice McLeod. He was long at the Bar of New Brunswick, he ie a very eminent judge; he has discharged his judicial duties with great ability, and I have nothing to eay against him personally. But the trouble in regard to the investigation that took place before those two gentlemen was that there w'as no counsel to represent the public-no- counsel to represent the other side. I would not trust the Angel Gabriel to come to a proper conclusion in regard to a question unless both sides were fairly represented.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: What side did Mr. Teed represent ?
Mr. Teed-
Oh, oh.
Mr. Teed is one of the warmest Conservatives in the province of New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: What has that to do with the matter?
Mr. Teed was no doubt employed because he was-
Because he was an honest man.
He was employed because it was felt he would aid the commissioners.
Who employed him?
I have no doubt the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) suggested his appointment.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member forgets that the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) stated that Mr. Teed was employed by Sir Ezekiel McLeod.

I have no doubt he was suggested by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries as a gentleman desirable to appoint for the purpoSk of aiding the commissioners. But you cannot have an investigation which can be depended upon unless you have both sides of the question fairly represented. Counsel was not present to represent the people and to sustain the view presented by Mr. Justice Galt, to see that all evidence which would have a bearing upon the correctness or otherwise of his opinion was fairly presented before the commission. You must have that in order to have a proper investigation.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We appointed counsel to . assist the commission. The commission was representing the people and no one else. Consequently counsel represented the people. If we were to appoint counsel on one side as against the other, then we would have to appoint counsel for Mr. Rogers. Mr. Rogers had his own counsel. Why did not the Government of Manitoba follow the same course?

I am not concerned with the Government of Manitoba. They appointed a commissioner who investigated the matter, and if there was not the fullest opportunity given to Mr. Rogers to be represented by counsel, then the commission was very greatly at fault.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: You do not answer the question.
After all, it is simply a question of the evidence. The matter is still for Parliament to deal with if it chooses to do so.
I understand my hon. friend from St. John has known Chief Justice McLeod for a great number of years.
Yes.-

I do not know him,
but I ask my hon. friend: Is Chief Justice

McLeod a man who would sign a report without knowing and approving its contents?

I have known very
eminent judges-
What about this particular judge?

I have known very
eminent judges, judges quite as eminent as Chief Justice McLeod who have been greatly misled by counsel.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Would Mr. Teed mislead him?	,

If you have a counsel,
no matter how honest he may be, whose inclination was to present views favourable, to those who employed him, it is easy for him to lead a judge into error.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Would Mr Teed mislead Chief Justice McLeod when Chief Justice McLeod employed him? That is a fair question.

My hon. friend is trespassing upon the credulity of this House, if he thinks that we shall believe that Mr. Teed was not appointed because it was -known that he was in sympathy with this Government; that he would be in sympat1 with Mr. Rogers.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) said that he was appointed by Chief Justice McLeod, and he was right. Why would Chief Justice McLeod appoint him if he thought he was favourable to this Government?

I have no doubt he was recommended by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries-. As I have said before, I would not rely upon the judgment of any jud#e, no matter how impartial, how eminent, unless opposing counsel were present. If there is only one counsel presenting one view, there is great danger of a misjud-ment. I -am sorry that my name has been dragged into this discussion. I am rather a modest man, and I do not like my name unduly brought before the House or before the country.
Your leader introduced it.

No, it was the Solicitor General who said that the Government was taking a different course to-day from the course taken in 1909. That was the first time my name was introduced, and it has
been bandied about rather freely since then. My hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) says that I stand guilty today before the people of this country because I did not adopt the machinery and get thoroughly whitewashed. I could have had that done, I suppose.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: What did the House of Commons do?

If I had written my
loader saying to him: I want you to appoint two judges and I will suggest-
And a lawyer.

-I would like you to appoint a lawyer, and I have in mind -a lawyer, very eminent, whose" eyes are directed towards the position of Chief Justice of my province, who will do me justice in any case, I would like you to appoint him to assist those commissioners in the investigation. In that case, I have no doubt the lime and the liquid would have been splendidly mixed and a good brush put into play, and I should have received a good coat of whitewash.
You certainly need one.

But I preferred not to do that. I thought it much better that my trial -should take place in the light of day, in the presence of the whole people of this country, that there should not be a commission that would sit secretly on my case. That is what I thought. And when my hon. friend the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) made a charge against me in the House based on the' Landry report, so-called, as those who were present will remember, the Speaker ruled that he had no right to do so and that the matter must come up in a different way. My right hon. leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who was then leader of the Government, stated, and I repeated what he stated, that we would take no technical objection, that we wanted the fullest possible inquiry and the most complete investigation. We wanted Parliament to have the evidence upon which this charge was based. The Speaker said that it was irregular for my hon. friend to bring the matter up in that way, but that if we consented, he would allow the matter to proceed.
You did not give Parliament any evidence.

When the present Minister of Labour made certain statements, I



said-and Hansard shows it-that the evidence did not support his statements, and he answered with indignation, "I have nothing to do with the evidence, nothing whatever, I rely upon this judgment of the court." My hon. friend rather questioned that to-day.
You had nothing more to do with he evidence than I had.

This is what he said- (Hansard, 1909, P. 5655):
' Mr. Pugsley:	My. hon. friend- must pardon
me. I say that there is nothing whatever in the evidence which would justify a statement of that kind, and the statement is absolutely untrue.
Mr. Crothers:	I am not here for the purpose
of discussing the evidence in this case.
And it was he who was prosecuting; it was he who was making the charge that was to drive me out of the Government and out of public life, if possible. He had nothing to do with the evidence, he said. He relied upon the judgment of the court. It did not concern him whether the evidence supported that judgment or not, or whether it was false or not; he had nothing to do with it. To continue:
Mr. Pugsley:	I am not surprised at that.
Mr. Crothers:	I am here standing on the
judgment of a court.
When I came to make my defence I relied upon such evidence as I had.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: You did not read -any.
I did. I quoted many parts of it. I said I had only two volumes of it, and that was all I could get. I said there was more than that.
You said you would not use the evidence at all.

I said that the Government had been asked to submit the evidence to the provincial legislature so that we could get a copy of it, but that request was refused. But a friend of mine, acting as counsel for the commissioners, had had the evidence taken by a stenographer, and he sent me a typewritten copy of part of it. That I used, and with that evidence I was able to show that in upwards of twenty instances the report was absolutely contradicted by the evidence, and in a great' many other cases not supported by the evidence. I am not going to refer to it particularly to-day, because I do not want to follow my hon. friend from Calgary and take up a great deal of the time of the House, but I remember that I called atten-

tion to one statement in the report, that the evidence had been conclusive that a certain act of wrong-doing had been committed. I made the -statement that it was absolutely untrue, that it showed the partisan character of these commissioners, and that so -far from it being the case, the evidence was absolutely the other way. Now my hon. friend says that they wanted to try me by the evidence. Let us see for a moment. To- begin with, we have the statement which my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition read on the 6th of August. Then we have the statement of the present distinguished Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) in a letter to Hon. Mr. Hazen, then Premier of New Brunswick, in which, referring to the matter, he said:
He will say that the report is not based on evidence and that he will, after getting a copy of the evidence, issue a statement showing this to be so. That will be his defence. We propose to get after him here before he gets a copy of the evidence.
Who was the hon. gentleman selected to get after me before I got a copy of the report? It was my hon. friend the present Minister of Labour who lent himself to that design of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. They were going to try to drive me from the Government, and if possible, from public life, before I could get a copy of the evidence.

You had a copy and
you did not read it.

But my hon. friend
thought I had not. He was doing what the Minister of Trade and Commerce had written to Mr. Hazen that, they would try to do; he lent himself to that design, in which, I am happy to say, he did not succeed. We have the further fact that the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries knerw th-jjt it was the intention to get after me before I got a copy of the evidence. That was why they refused to submit the evidence to the provincial legislature, because if they submitted it they knew I would get a copy, and they thought I had no copy of it. The present -Minister of Marine and Fisheries, then Premier of New Brunswick, knew that that was the intention, because he had the letter from the present Minister of Trade and Commerce before he sent the report up to Ottawa to be used by my hon. friend in the improper way in which he sought to use it, and did use it. What evidence had Mr. Hazen -at that time, when he knew he was sending a damnable and false report to Ottawa for the purpose of accomplishing the

design he had in view? He had in his possession a letter from Mr. Powell, a very distinguished Conservative employed hy the Provincial Government-paid by the Provincial Government-to assist the commissioners, just as Mr. Teed is to be paid by the Government of Canada to assist these commissioners; he was equally eminent, equally honourable, equally high in the public esteem, equally prominent in the Conservative party-in fact, I would think that Mr. Pewell was even more prominent in the Conservative party than Mr. Teed, because he had been a member of his Parliament, and to-day he occupies a high-salaried position under this Government as a member of the Great Waterways -Commission! He also says that he was doing a great deal of the work which, I presume, Mr. Teed was employed to dov. in connection with this commission; that is to say, he assisted in drawing up many parts of the report. Mr. Powell, in his letter to Mr. Hazen of March 31, 1909, said, among other things:
Another matter which I am sorry has gone in as it did inasmuch as it will give the Opposition press an opportunity to make an attack on the commissioners, is the statement at the bottom of page 18 and top of page 19 to the effect that it appears conclusively from the evidence that the whole $250,000 par value of the 3 per cent bonds had been guaranteed and delivered to the company up to August 6, 1903.
When I was making my speech I referred to the evidence and said it was absolutely false-not only unsupported by the evidence hut absolutely contradicted by it. I did not know then that when Mr. Hazen sent that report here he knew it was false, and that he had a statement from Mr. Powell to the effect that it was false. I simply had to present the matter to the House from my own standpoint, and as I knew the evidence would show it to be. Mr. Powell goes on:
The only evidence to that effect was an impression Mr. Shadbolt had that the whole $250 000 of 3 per cent bonds which were delivered to him at that time had the provincial guarantee on them. Mr. Shadbolt may have been right in his impression, but the statement is not consistent with the Order in Council with reference to guaranteeing the bonds.
A little further on he says:
I drafted the portion of the report referring to the guaranteeing of the bonds, hut Judge Landry himself changed it in the respects I have mentioned. Fortunately the fellows on the other side will know nothing about the matter, and if the statement is challenged the reporter has Mr. Shadbolt's evidence much stronger than he gave it.
What does that mean?

It means that the Government reporter had changed the evidence from what was given, and he would find in the typewritten copy a report of evidence which had never been sworn to by the witness. It also means that when Mr. Hazen sent that statement forward to Sir George Foster, Mr. Hazen knew the report was false. It means he knew that the stenographer had the evidence in his transcribed copy much stronger than it had been given and he sends this false report forward to Sir George Foster, and Sir George Foster hands it to the present Minister of Labour in order to present those falsehoods before the members of this House and before the people of this country and to ask that I should be condemned. You have in that evidence of conspiracy in which four prominent members of the Conservative party were engaged. Perhaps I should not in this House call it a conspiracy-I will call it an enterprise.
The Minister of Labour would not be engaged in any enterprise.

Engaged in that enterprise was the present Senator, Hon. Mr. Fowler, who wrote Mr. Hazen recommending certain gentlemen as commissioners and who said that this was a very important thing for them and he believed that the "Genial William"-meaning myself-
That was the only truth in it.

-Could be driven out of business if the thing was handled properly, and he suggests how it might be handled. Then we have Mr. Powell, appointed to the same position as Mr. Teed was appointed to in connection with this commission, not only taking part in the presentation of the evidence, but taking part in the making up of the opinion. We find him writing to Mr. Hazen, and calling his attention to an important matter in which the report is false, and saying that fortunately if it comes up the fellows on the other side would not know anything about it, and if it is questioned the reporter has it down already much stronger than the witness gave it. We find Sir George Foster handing this report to my hon. friend the present Minister of Labour to act upon. Notwithstanding all this, these gentlemen try to make the committee believe that they acted in a very different way, and in a very much better way in regard to Mr. Rogers than the way followed in 1909 by the supporters of the former government. I should be very sorry indeed

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Before the committee
rises it seems to me that on the stand taken by the hon. member for .Carleton and the hon. member for St. John there should be no objection to the item going through. As I understand it, they want a chance to discuss the McLeod-Tellier report.

I never asked for a
chance to discuss the McLeod-Tellier report, and I have been persistently opposed to discussing the Galt report, il felt it was a matter that should not have been brought up here at all. I object, however, to the 
item being voted to-night in view of the attitude assumed by the Minister of Labour and to a great extent by the Solicitor General, that there was no evidence on which the Galt report could be sustained. Before the -item is voted, I think there should be an opportunity of discussing the evidence.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I thunk the hon. gentleman misrepresents me. I have not asked for this vote on the ground that there is no evidence to justify the Galt report. I distinctly took the other ground; I should ask for the vote just the same if the finding were the other way. I never assented to anything on my own responsibility. I simply say what the tribunal found. The hon. member for Carleton stated very clearly and rightly that the report of Mr. Justice Galt being out, it was impossible to proceed, and we know that the proper course was to have an investigation, and the minister step out in the meantime. That being so, that is all the reason there is for this item. If, by reason of anything that arose in this debate, hon. gentlemen opposite desire to discuss the McLeod-Tellier report, I will undertake that their right to do so will not be prejudiced by this item going through. But we are sincerely anxious to get on as rapidly as we can. I do not want to put my own inconvenience as too important before the committee, -but I do not want to come back and have -an afternoon or night spent on this item for the purpose of a discussion at which I do not need to be present. Is there any objection to the motion being withdrawn and the item passing, it being understood that if hon. gentlemen wish to discuss the McLeod-Tellier report, they will be given, I am pretty sure, by the Prime Minister, the -right to do so. At all events, their-right to do so will not be prejudiced by the item going through.
We can take a vote upon it.
